newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist tired but pleased with solo trip.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist tired but pleased with solo trip.

text.p: U.S. adventurer Steve Fossett said on Monday he was exhausted but satisfied after landing his balloon in northern India, halfway around the world from his U.S. starting point but short of his goal.

"It was a very good trip," Fossett told Reuters by telephone from Peeparpur village, some 550 km (330 miles) southeast of Delhi. "I wish I could have made the biggest achievement and flown around the world. But this is also successful."

In his first interview since landing in Nonkhar village at 0735 GMT on Monday, Fossett said he was pleased he broke two records during his six-day flight -- the longest distance covered by a balloon and the longest time spent in the air.

He said he landed safely in a field and was not injured, but his balloon ripped when it snagged in a tree. "It was a safe but rough landing," he said, adding that the wind was blowing at 24 km (15 miles) an hour. "It probably ruined the balloon."

Asked if he was disappointed he did not achieve his goal of circling the globe, Fossett said: "Not really. This was also successful. It showed we are very close to being able to fly around the world."

Fossett, who said he had miscalculated the amount of fuel needed and did not get enough sleep, was asked when he might make a fresh bid to fly around the world nonstop. "I haven't had a chance to think of that," he said. "I just have to reflect."

The 52-year-old commodity broker-turned-adventurer said about 100 villagers greeted him after he landed and helped him to begin packing his equipment. The first police showed up some two hours later, he said.
"The people have been very nice," he said, speaking from a police station some 20 km (12 miles) from the landing site.
But he had been unable to find a telephone which would allow him to call his mission control in Chicago. He had also lost contact with a support team that had been accompanying him in an airplane.
"The support team can't find me," he said, asking to have a message that he was safe transmitted to Chicago.
Fossett said he had enough fuel to make it eastwards halfway across the Pacific if he had continued, but that the winds might have carried him northward towards the Himalaya mountains and China.
"I wanted to land in a valley near the Ganges River," he said. "I didn't want to continue on over the Himalayas and didn't want to land in China because I did not have permission to land there."
Asked how he felt when he landed, Fossett said: "I usually like to do it in calm conditions. This was a much more difficult landing."
He said his health was good as he had eaten ready-made meals. But he was short of sleep.

"I didn't get enough sleep. That was one of the problems as I had to average two hours a day, just a short nap. I had hoped to get four hours," he said, adding that he had to be regularly in touch with air traffic controllers during his flight.
He said his cabin heaters did not work above 19,000 feet (5,800 metres), where the temperature was about minus 16 Fahrenheit (minus 27 Celsius) and more favourable winds blew.
Fossett said he would finish packing his balloon on Tuesday and probably go to Delhi before heading back to the United States in two or three days.
"We did have a very good system," he said. "It would require only a few more changes -- a bigger balloon, more fuel and a little bit more luck."
